Thanks to the reviewer for his comments.

`•	The baseline methods for continual learning used in experiments are a little outdated. According to Sec. 5.1, most baseline methods were published before 2021. More recent methods (in 2021 and 2022) should be included in the experiment part.`

As suggested, we provide results using additional baselines including:

- [1] Prakhar Kaushik et al. “Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting and Remembering in Continual Learning with Optimal Relevance Mapping.”, Workshop on Meta-Learning at NeurIPS, 2021.

- [2] Mirzadeh, S. et al. “Linear Mode Connectivity in Multitask and Continual Learning.”, ArXiv, abs/2010.04495, 2021.

- [3] Mirzadeh, Seyed Iman et al. “Dropout as an Implicit Gating Mechanism For Continual Learning.” 2020 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW) (2020): 945-951.

We use equivalent setup as we have in our evaluation for fair comparison. We measure and report the accuracy (ACC) over 3 runs.

We found out that [1] works well with larger batch size (e.g. 256 as in the original paper). While with batch size of 10 (as in our approach) the method was not able to learn. In the multi-pass, we also noticed that this baseline [1] needs more epochs in order to achieve higher accuracy. In the results of the baseline [1] in the multi-pass continual learning regime, we set the number of passes, i.e., the number of epochs per task to 10 for [1], while for our method we set the number of epochs to 3. We set the number of passes, i.e., the number of epochs per task to 80 for [2], while for our method we set the number of epochs to 3. In the results of the baselines [2][3] in the continual learning regimes [2] [3] use batch size of 50. 

As we can see from the results, in the equivalent evaluation setup, our approach outperforms the related baselines.

`•	I wonder if the proposed method is still effective when it is combined with the SOTA methods for continual learning.`

Please see the response to Reviewer bUCm.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use group-wise normalization (using the scaling-only operation not the standardization operation) at the penultimate layer of the used neural network for continual learning. It analyzes the learning dynamics and claims that this group-wise normalization induces “soft” weighing during the backpropagation, and works like a competition between the subset of weights that connects to the corresponding groups. It evaluates the proposed method on various benchmarks, including MNIST (rotation and permutation),CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet under several continual learning setup. The results demonstrate the proposed method improves the performance of network for continual learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

1.The proposed method is simple, computation efficient and empirically improves the performance of network for continual learning, based on the experiments. 


2. I appreciate this paper conducted many experiments, even though I have concerns on the experimental setup and results. 



**Weaknesses:** 

1.The technical novelty and contributions are incremental. Normalization techniques have been explored for the continual learning tasks, e.g., continual normalization (CN) that combines group normalization (GN) and batch normalization (BN). This paper addresses to use group-wise normalization (using the scaling-only operation not the standardization operation) at the penultimate layer of the used neural network. It is unclear, why the operation is just the scaling operation of normalization? Does the standardization (centering+scaling, as group normalization does) works worse? I did find this paper discusses the learning dynamics in section 4.2 and shows the proposed group scaling (Eqn.1) induces back-propagation weighting with strength inversely
proportional to the norm of the unnormalized neuron activation in the group (Eqn.2). This learning dynamics indeed are widely discussed in previous work (the so-called scale-invariant property induced by the scaling operation of normalization, please refer to the corresponding section in [1]). Indeed, the original group normalization (using standardization operation) also has such a property. Why not use the standardization operation?
Besides, it is not clear why not add the proposed group-scaling method into the intermediate layers to replace the original normalization (e.g., BN) in the network. 



2.I have several concerns for the experiments. I think the main baseline for the experiments of this paper is the continual normalization (CN), since CN also is designed for continual learning, and uses group normalization warped in the CN module. This paper should follow the experiments/setups used in CN for comparison. However, this paper only compares the results to CN in Table 4 for CIFAR100 datasets. By comparing the results of Table 4 to the results shown in CN paper (Pham et al., 2022), I find that CN indeed has a RA (ACC) of 67.48, while this paper has a reproduction for CN of 60.18, which is a big gap. Besides, From Table 4, I find GNOR only has marginally better performance than BN, and BN even works better than CN, which seems to be inconsistent to the results shown in CN paper. I expect this paper can provide feedback for my concerns. 

3.I am not convinced by the competition mechanism. It seems just a conjecture. E.g, “In fact, the weighting induced by the group of neurons with the highest sparsity causes the directly connected subset of weights to receive ”most of the learning”, i.e. win the competition”. What is the definition of "win the competition", how does “win the competition” benefits the continual learning?


[1] Normalization Techniques in Training DNNs: Methodology, Analysis and Application, arxiv: 2009.12836

content.title: Response to Reviewer mEra Part 1
content.comment:
Thanks for the reviewer for the provided review.

`1.The technical novelty and contributions are incremental. Normalization techniques have been explored for the continual learning tasks, e.g., continual normalization (CN) that combines group normalization (GN) and batch normalization (BN). `

We agree that the authors in continual normalization (CN) explored/addressed normalization technique in a continual learning regime. However, we study different aspects, 
- our findings highlight a competition mechanism between the subset of weighs that connect to the penultimate layer in a relation to the group sparsity at the penultimate layer, and we believe pinpoint different, important/interesting and possibly overlooked properties relevant for continual learning, and our approach differs significantly then CN since
- we do not use parameters in our normalization,

making it more efficient.

`This paper addresses to use group-wise normalization (using the scaling-only operation not the standardization operation) at the penultimate layer of the used neural network. It is unclear, why the operation is just the scaling operation of normalization? Does the standardization (centering+scaling, as group normalization does) works worse? `

Empirically, we also evaluated with the standardization operation, but we got lower accuracy. We believe that this is due to the fact that the zero-mean normalization changes the sparsity level in a way that even if have sparse activation after the zero-mean normalization the sparsity level may increase. In addition, in the Appendix, we evaluated with “soft” and “hard” thresholding that follows or is before the actual normalization. Please have a look there for more details.

`I did find this paper discusses the learning dynamics in section 4.2 and shows the proposed group scaling (Eqn.1) induces back-propagation weighting with strength inversely proportional to the norm of the unnormalized neuron activation in the group (Eqn.2). This learning dynamics indeed are widely discussed in previous work (the so-called scale-invariant property induced by the scaling operation of normalization, please refer to the corresponding section in [1]).`

In [1], the authors have extensively and thoroughly studied/examined the effect of some normalization techniques in deep learning. However, they have not addressed continual learning and in particular forgetting. 

As we explain in the main text, without the normalization the sparsity level might be high, but the strength of the activations for the group of neurons might be low. Thus, the parameters connecting group of neurons at the penultimate layer and the previous layer (as well as the parameters of the network before the penultimate layer) might miss the required learning.

Here, we demonstrated in the single-pass CL at CIFAR 100 (please see Table 1) that with the group-wise normalization, the sparser groups of neurons cause “more learning” to be allocated for the directly connected corresponding subset of weights.  As we can see in Table 1, the gradient strength for the subsets of the corresponding weighs do not change when we do not use normalization, while the gradient strength for the subsets of the corresponding weighs is higher for the connecting groups with higher sparsity under group-wise normalization. 

`Besides, it is not clear why not add the proposed group-scaling method into the intermediate layers to replace the original normalization (e.g., BN) in the network.`

We have tried adding group-wise normalization on all of the feed-forward layers in the used networks. The results suggest that group-wise normalization only at the penultimate layer has the biggest effect. Please see the details in the Appendix.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1400 by Reviewer mEra

content.title: Response to Reviewer mEra Part 2
content.comment:
`2. I have several concerns for the experiments. I think the main baseline for the experiments of this paper is the continual normalization (CN), since CN also is designed for continual learning, and uses group normalization warped in the CN module. This paper should follow the experiments/setups used in CN for comparison. However, this paper only compares the results to CN in Table 4 for CIFAR100 datasets. By comparing the results of Table 4 to the results shown in CN paper (Pham et al., 2022), I find that CN indeed has a RA (ACC) of 67.48, while this paper has a reproduction for CN of 60.18, which is a big gap. Besides, From Table 4, I find GNOR only has marginally better performance than BN, and BN even works better than CN, which seems to be inconsistent to the results shown in CN paper. I expect this paper can provide feedback for my concerns.`

As mentioned in the main text Section 5.1, (subsection Used Neural Networks and Hyper-parameters), please note that we use a network consisting of 3 convolutional layers followed by 3 feed-forward linear layers for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 and a network consisting of 4 convolutional layers followed by 3 feed-forward linear layers for TynyImageNet as in (Gupta et al., 2020). While in the paper by Pham et al., 2022, the authors use a version of ResNet-18 that is much larger then the neural networks used here. 

We also have to point out that since we use gnor only at the penultimate layer, we use BN, LN, GN and CN in exact setup (applied only at the penultimate layer) for fair comparison.

`3. I am not convinced by the competition mechanism. It seems just a conjecture. E.g, “In fact, the weighting induced by the group of neurons with the highest sparsity causes the directly connected subset of weights to receive ”most of the learning”, i.e. win the competition”. What is the definition of "win the competition", how does “win the competition” benefits the continual learning?`


We mean “wins the competition” in a sense that these subsets of weights receive more learning measured by the magnitude of the corresponding gradients during learning, while these gradients have similar sparsity levels under group-wise normalization. 

To explain further the benefit of our very simple approach note that we use similar assumptions as presented and verified in the LWTA paper. We assume that a sparser activation for a group of neurons represents a more distinctive feature for the corresponding input sample (or batch of samples).  Therefore, our argumentation is that when the learning is more focused on the subset of weights that directly connect to the corresponding sparse groups of neurons, we have less unwanted interference and neural network parameters override, since these parameters are considered/assumed to be more important for that sample (or batch of samples). On the contrarily when the learning is not focused (in the case when we do not use any other mechanisms) it might happen that we override parameters that are important for other samples (tasks). Thus, our approach with its learning dynamics, benefits CL in avoiding parameter overriding and thus forgetting. 

Among all the results/ ablations/ comparisons that this paper presents, the results in Table 1 and Table 2 answer the questions why the approach works and the significance of gnor. Thus, our results demonstrate the above claims.

We believe we cleared out more on the technical contribution, the intuition behind the approach as well as the concerns about the experiments.

Please let us know if there are any other questions/concerns.

content.title: Response to the comment after the rebuttal
content.comment:
Thanks for the rebuttal comment.
I would like to point out that

1. While we agree that the proposed gnor is very simple and easy to implement, we believe our findings pinpoint different, important/interesting and possibly overlooked properties relevant for continual learning, thus together with the extensive evaluation provide solid contribution. Although gnor can be seen as a normalization, we were interested and focused on it's learning dynamics and the induced competitive nature, which is very different then the CN paper, while at the same time we believe we demonstrated gnor's effectiveness and gnor's ability in overcoming forgetting. 
2. We include and provide results about why the algorithm works in the main paper, especially why the learning dynamics imposed by the proposed gnor prevents forgetting, where we explain the connection between (a) the sparsity of group of neurons at the penultimate layer and (b) the average gradient sparsity for subset of weighs that connect the corresponding group of neurons at the penultimate layer with the layer before and (c) the average gradient strength for subset of weighs that connect the corresponding group of neurons at the penultimate layer with the layer before (we believe all the details are given in the paper). 
3. We compare with existing methods (ER, ICARL, GEM, AGEM, MER, META-BGD, LA-MAML, LWTA) using convolutional networks as in La-Maml paper (G. Gupta at al., 2020) on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and TinyImageNet, where we show improvements.
4. We compare with normalization methods (BN, GN, LN, CN, l_inf-norm, l_1-norm) using convolutional networks as in La-Maml paper (G. Gupta at al., 2020) on the CIFAR10 where we show improvements.
5. We compare with CN in the equivalent setup as in the CN paper (Q Pham at al. ICLR 2022) using ResNet architecture (please see in our response here) on the CIFAR10 and Split Tiny IMN which was also asked from the reviewer, where we show significant improvements.
6. We provide additional comparison to [1], [2] and [3] as more recent methods in the evaluation setup as in the La-Maml paper (G. Gupta at al., 2020), as requested by the reviewers and demonstrated superior results.
7. We added gnor at the penultimate layer in La-Maml and GEM and evaluated in the equivalent setup as in the La-Maml paper (G. Gupta at al., 2020) (please see in our response here), where we show improvement.
8. We compare in task-agnostic continual learning regime and show the advantages (main text of the paper).
9. We provide ablation about the influence and impact our approach as well as additional results in the Appendix.

We would appreciate that the reviewer 
- Pinpoints what other concerns it has about the paper and 
- Why the reviewer is not convinced in the explanations (backed up by the extensive empirical results) why gnors prevents catastrophic forgetting.

References
- [1] Prakhar Kaushik et al. “Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting and Remembering in Continual Learning with Optimal Relevance Mapping.”, Workshop on Meta-Learning at NeurIPS, 2021.
- [2] Mirzadeh, S. et al. “Linear Mode Connectivity in Multitask and Continual Learning.”, ArXiv, abs/2010.04495, 2021.
- [3] Mirzadeh, Seyed Iman et al. “Dropout as an Implicit Gating Mechanism For Continual Learning.” 2020 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW) (2020): 945-951.
- G. Gupta, Karmesh Yadav, and L. Paull. Look-ahead meta learning for continual learning. In NeurIPS, 2020.
- Quang Pham and Chenghao Liu and Steven HOI, Continual Normalization: Rethinking Batch Normalization for Online Continual Learning, ICLR 2022

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, authors propose a novel normalization technique (gnor) for addressing the catastrophic problem in continual learning (CL). Motivated by the usefulness of the sparse representation in CL, the proposed normalization makes the features of penultimate layer being sparse, so that the gradient of linear activation with respect to the penultimate features also becomes sparse, and as a result, a learner can drastically decrease the interference from learning a new task. In the experiment, the authors show that using gnor makes the gradient of features on penultimate layer being sparse, and the results for the average accuracy are comparable to state-of-the-art methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Here are Pros and Cons about the proposed method.

**Pros:**

P1. The proposed normalization technique (gnor) is easy to apply, and extremely simple. Unlike previous methods (Javed & White, 2019 / Jung et al., 2020) that used meta-learning or group sparse regularization for achieving the sparsity of the representation, the proposed approach just used the normalization of the features on penultimate layer. 

**Cons:**

C1. It would be better to carry out experiments using large-scale architectures (e.g. Resnet-18) equipped with batch-normalization (BN). I think gnor should be compatible with widely used normalization methods.

C2. The increase of the average accuracy compared to the baseline methods is somewhat marginal. It would be better if gnor can be applied to other baselines (e.g. La-MAML or GEM) so that gnor can increase the performance of the baselines

C3. The explanations on the results in Table are not clear. Why the representations have less overlap? Is it due to the competition mechanism?

**Minor comments**

In my humble opinion, there are some minor typos in the manuscript

In page 1, "had-crafted" --> "hand-crafted"

In page 2 (Related Work), "resent" --> "recent"

In page 3 (Related Work), "nether" --> "neither"

In Appendix D, I think there are some unintentional errors in Latex source when writing the PyTorch implementation of the group-wise normalization.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method is simple and effective, but it cannot be a significantly novel approach. The proposed normalization technique is developed based on LWTA, and the overall formulation is also similar to LWTA.
content.summary_of_the_review: Though the proposed method is simple and easy to apply, the contributions are somewhat limited. First, the performance improvement compared to the baselines is marginal. Second, there is no guarantee that gnor can be compatible with other normalization schemes.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer bUCm
content.comment:
Thanks to the reviewer for the provided feedback.

`C1. It would be better to carry out experiments using large-scale architectures (e.g. Resnet-18) equipped with batch-normalization (BN). I think gnor should be compatible with widely used normalization methods. `

Please note that in our extensive evaluation we use much smaller and more efficient neural networks (G. Gupta at al., 2022) compared to the Res-Net-18 network. Nonetheless, we are evaluating additional experiments using the ResNet-18 neural network architectures as soon as we get the additional results, we will share them here.

Using ResNet-18 as in the Continual Normalization (CN) paper on the CIFAR-10 we got comparable accuracy of 85% when we use gnor at all layers and at the penultimate layer (and with a small modification of the ReNet-18) in the equivalent setup as in the CN paper, while we do not use the additional CN learning parameters.


`C2. The increase of the average accuracy compared to the baseline methods is somewhat marginal. It would be better if gnor can be applied to other baselines (e.g. La-MAML or GEM) so that gnor can increase the performance of the baselines`

Please note that in the result tables, if we compute the average improvement of the proposed method compared to the best results from the baselines among all results in the presented Tables, we have an average improvement of around __2%__ (max improvement __4.5%__ on multi-pass CL setup at TinyImageNet, please see __Table 7__, min improvement __.76%__, on single-pass CL setup at CIFAR100).

Regarding the compatibility with existing state-of-the-art methods, we have experimented with gnor at the penultimate layer for 
- La-MAML and 
- GEM,

using the neural network architecture as in (G. Gupta at al., 2022) for the CIFAR100 and TynyImageNet in the single-pass CL regime and we have obtained average improvements of around __2%__.

`C3. The explanations on the results in Table are not clear. Why the representations have less overlap? Is it due to the competition mechanism?`

Regarding the evaluation setup and results for Tables 1 and 2, we plan to add more explanation and details as well as sharpen the exposition.

We further explain the small representaion overlap/override in the following way. First, we demonstrated in the single-pass CL at CIFAR 100 (please see Table 1) that with the group-wise normalization the sparser groups of neurons, cause to have “more learning” for the directly connected corresponding subset of weights.  As we can see in Table 1, the gradient strength for the subsets of the corresponding weighs do not change when we do not use normalization, while the gradient strength for the subsets of the corresponding weighs is higher for the connecting groups with higher sparsity under group-wise normalization. 

We assume that a sparser activation for a group of neurons represents a more distinctive feature for the corresponding input sample (or batch of samples).  Therefore, our argumentation is that when the learning is more focused (as it is the case with our approach) on the subset of weights that directly connect to the corresponding sparse groups of neurons, we have less unwanted interference and neural network parameters override, since these parameters are considered/assumed to be more important for that sample (or batch of samples). On the contrarily when the learning is not focused (in the case when we do not use any other mechanisms) it might happen that we override parameters that are important for other samples (tasks). As we demonstrate by the results on Table 2, in the single-pass CL at CIFAR 100, this also impacts the override and overlap of the representaion at the penultimate layer.

Please let us know if there are any other questions/concerns.

G. Gupta, Karmesh Yadav, and L. Paull. Look-ahead meta learning for continual learning. In NeurIPS, 2020.

`Minor comments`

Thanks for pointing out the minor comments/typos and unintentional errors, we will fix them.


`Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility:The proposed method is simple and effective, but it cannot be a significantly novel approach. The proposed normalization technique is developed based on LWTA, and the overall formulation is also similar to LWTA.`

We agree that we have some similarities with LWTA, like the fact that the operation is preformed locally, on a group of neuron activations. However, in LWTA the operation is maximum, here we used l_2 norm normalization. Maybe more importantly, the effects as well as the learning dynamics of using LWTA and gnor are completely different. Please see more details in the paper and its Appendix.

Regarding the stated line of the reasoning, similarly, we can say that Bach Norm (BN), Instance Norm (IN), Layer Norm (LN), Group Norm (GN) or Continual Norm (CN) are using ”overall similar formulation”, but all of them lead to a very different effect, and have their own merits, while published as standalone papers.

content.comment:
Thank you for the comments on the questions.

The authors addressed the questions, but to me, the work is still not convincing regarding the answers on the question C2 and Novelty. Though applying gnor is simple, in my opinion, the performance improvement is still somewhat marginal, and gnor seems to have marginal modification over LWTA because the operation in LWTA is simply replaced with L2 normalization.

Therefore, I'll keep my score to 5.

content.title: Rebuttal Summary
content.comment:
We want to thank again the Reviewers for the provided feedback, recognizing the simple and efficient approach presented in this work, and our effort in providing a comprehensive empirical study. We highlight our finding about a competition mechanism between the subset of weighs that connect to the penultimate layer in a relation to the group sparsity at the penultimate layer, and we believe pinpoint different, important/interesting and possibly overlooked properties relevant for continual learning. We also are with the opinion that we have significant differences to CN, since we do not use parameters in our normalization, making the approach presented here slightly more efficient.

In the following, we give a summary about the rebuttal modification/changes that we addressed to further increase and improve the paper quality thanks to the reviewer’s feedback (including the new results, the paper has now 8 ablation results, compares with 15 different approaches and has additional results in the appendix, while we open source our code implementation).

1. As suggested by the reviewers, we provide additional results, comparisons with additional recent work (we shared the results in the comment to Reviewer with ID Sa3c and will include them in the Appendix), additional comparative result to the CN paper addressing the Reviewers recommendations about results using ResNet-18 (which we will also include in the Appendix) as well as results that give slight improvement on existing methods (La-MAML and GEM) when using gnor.

2. We corrected the typos and the unwanted/unaware error for the pseudocode of gnor.

3. We gave our best to clear out misunderstanding, explain more about the results and pinpointed to overlooked description/explanation in the paper as well as directed the Reviewers to the additional empirical evaluations in the Appendix that support the claims of our work.

4. As noted by the reviewers, we expanded the discussion\explanation that directly supports our claim with empirical result that after the group-wise normalization the subsets of weighs that connect to the groups of neurons with high sparsity  receive "more learning". This is important since when the learning is more focused on the subset of weights that directly connect to the corresponding
sparse groups of neurons, we have less unwanted interference and neural network parameters override. Since such "guided" gradient for these parameters (which affect also the gradient for the parameters before them) are considered/assumed to be more important for that sample (or batch of samples). On the contrarily when the learning is not focused (in the case when we do not use any other mechanisms) it might happen that we override parameters that are important for other samples (tasks). As empirically verified this leads to less unwanted interference and less neural network parameters override. Moreover, we demonstrate that it leads and accommodates balanced use of the network capacity, achieves stable and efficient feature use, allows to discriminate more between the different representations and enables less forgetting. We believe that this adds to the paper quality and makes the paper more thorough and complete. We plan to further sharpen the explanation about the motivation behind our work.

We hope that we have answered the raised question by the reviewers. Please let us know if there are other questions/misunderstanding or need for additional clarification.

content.title: Additional Comparative Results using Res-Net on CIFAR 10 and Split Tiny IMN
content.comment:
As suggested, we have done additional experiments using ResNet neural network architecture (as in Quang P. et al.)  on the 

- CIFAR10 and 
- Split Tiny IMN data sets. 

We follow the continual learning setup as in Quang P. et al. We evaluated using the equivalent neural network architecture as in Quang P. et al. where we used

1. Bach Normalization (bn) at all network layers, without gnor at the penultimate layer (__bn__).
2. bn at all network layers with gnor at the penultimate layer (__bn+gnor__) and modify the final linear layer to be without bias.
3. Continual Normalization (cn)  by Quang P. et al. at all network layers without gnor at the penultimate layer (__cn__).
4. cn at all network layers with gnor at the penultimate layer (__cn+gnor__) and modify the final linear layer to be without bias.

To run the experiments, we used the official github implementation (https://github.com/phquang/Continual-Normalization) accompanying the paper by Quang P. et al. while as learning algorithm we used der++. All results are an average of 4 runs.

On the CIFAR10, we used the equivalent parameter setup as provided for der++ at https://github.com/phquang/Continual-Normalization. Below, we show the results. In bn+gnor and cn+gnor, for the gnor normalization at the penultimate layer, we used 32 groups of 16 elements each.

|   |  |  |  CIFAR10 |  |   | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |   | Class-il | |  Task-il | |
| Buffer  |  Method   | Acc. | FT |  Acc. | FT |
|500 |  |  |  |  |  |
|| cn | __51.7±1.9__ | 28.2±4.0 | __86.2±2.2__ | 2.0±1.3 |
|| bn | 48.9±4.5 | 33.6±5.8 | 82.6±2.3 | 3.2±1.9 |
|| cn+gnor | 50.3±3.0 | 31.8±13.8 | __86.0±0.6__ | 2.2±1.7 |
|| bn+gnor | 49.1±49.9 | 32.7±190.3 | 83.2±14.9 | 5.8±79.6 |
|2560 |  |  |  |  |  |

||bn  | 52.3±4.6 | 29.7±6.1 | 86.6±1.6 | 0.9±0.7 |
||cn+gnor |55.8±6.8 | 28.2±2.1 | 88.5±2.1 | 2.7±0.7 |

||bn+gnor |__62.2±0.7__ | 18.2±52.9 | __90.5±0.4__ | 0.4±7.7 |

As we can see from the results, bn+gnor provides significant improvements at the class-incremental (Class-il) and the task-incremental (Task-il) continual learning regimes. bn+gnor provides improved performance of around __4%__ compared to cn when using buffers of 2560 and 5160 in the class-incremental regime, while at the same time bn+gnor provides improved performance of __1.2%__ and __2.2%__ compared to cn when using buffers of 2560 and 5160 in the task-incremental regime.

On the Split Tiny IMN, we used the equivalent parameter setup as provided for der++ at https://github.com/phquang/Continual-Normalization with the following changes, learning rate .22, alpha=.075 and beta=1 for all of the used buffer sizes. Below, we show the results. In bn+gnor and cn+gnor, for the gnor normalization at the penultimate layer, we used 64 groups of 8 elements each.

As we can see from the results on this data set, both cn+gnor and bn+gnor provide improvements in the class-incremental (Class-il) and the task-incremental (Task-il) continual learning regimes. cn+gnor and bn+gnor provide improved performance of around __4%__ and __5%__ compared to cn when using buffers of 2560 and 5160, respectively, in the class-incremental regime. cn+gnor provides comparable performance compared to cn when using buffers of 500, 2560 and 5160 in the task-incremental regime.

We believe that these results additionally support out claims and increase further the quality of the paper.

Quang Pham and Chenghao Liu and Steven HOI, Continual Normalization: Rethinking Batch Normalization for Online Continual Learning, ICLR 2022
